How teams remember technical documents

This fictional research report describes a small pilot comparing two ways of reviewing technical documents.
Forty volunteers from one software team read a design document and answered questions about it the following day.
Half the volunteers received a short written summary alongside the document. The other half received only the original document.
The group with a summary recalled more of the document's main tradeoffs on the next-day questionnaire.
The pilot did not measure whether summaries improved the quality of actual engineering decisions.
The summary group also reported spending less time reviewing the material, but review time was self-reported rather than measured.
Participants were assigned by availability, not randomly, so differences between the groups may have influenced the findings.
All volunteers came from one team already familiar with the subject. The result may not apply to beginners or other organizations.
The authors argue that a summary can help orient readers before they examine the full source.
They caution that compression can remove important qualifications and that readers should not treat summaries as complete substitutes for the source.
One example in the report concerns a proposed database migration: remembering the headline benefit without the rollback condition would leave the reader with an incomplete understanding.
The report distinguishes recalling facts from understanding uncertainty. The questionnaire mainly tested recall and offered limited evidence about the latter.
The pilot does not establish that audio summaries perform better than written summaries; audio was not included in the comparison.
A small number of participants preferred the original document because they wanted to inspect assumptions and supporting details directly.
The report leaves open whether repeated use would change reading habits or increase reliance on incomplete summaries.
These findings are preliminary observations from a fictional pilot, not a validated benchmark or a general claim about all readers.
